sources.title: Box Office: ‘Digger’ Nosediving With $3.4 Million on Opening Day, ‘Verity’ Lands at No. 1 With $15.1 Million on Friday

discussion.body: A GQ cover and a spirit-tunnel bit are evidence of effort, not of demand. Studios can buy attention; they can't buy the second weekend.
Or the playbook is just what a studio does now, whatever the movie is. The more interesting question is whether that press tour reached the people who actually go see an R-rated black comedy.

items.title: Tom Cruise's Full-Court Press Tour Didn't Save 'Digger' From a $3.4 Million Friday
items.body: Warner Bros.' R-rated black comedy “Digger” took in $3.4 million from 3,321 North American theaters on its opening Friday, Variety reports. The press push behind it was built around Tom Cruise: a GQ cover, an appearance on the “New Heights” podcast, and a “Risky Business”-inspired walk down the “Jennifer Hudson Show” spirit tunnel. Variety's read is blunt — none of that kept the film from flatlining. A wide release spreads a modest gross very thin, and the Friday number is a snapshot of turnout rather than a verdict on the film. Opening-day figures measure how many people showed up, not whether anyone else will.

sources.title: Canada bet billions on an EV boom. Was it too much, too soon?

discussion.body: The bet may not have been wrong about electric vehicles existing. It looks wrong about the pace — if weaker-than-expected demand is the thread running through all of it.
“Substantially changed” is doing quiet work in that list. A project that gets re-scoped is not the same as one that is cancelled, and the story counts both.

items.title: Canada's EV Bet Runs Into Weaker-Than-Expected Demand
items.body: Federal and provincial governments bet billions on the rapid rise of the electric vehicle industry. CBC reports that major EV and battery projects in Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia have since been delayed, cancelled, suspended or substantially changed — and in one case gone bankrupt — as automakers and suppliers adjust to weaker-than-anticipated demand. That list is not a single verdict. A delay, a suspension and a bankruptcy are different outcomes, and counting them in one column flattens the difference. The common thread the reporting identifies is demand that arrived weaker than planned, which turns a question about industrial policy into a question about timing.

sources.title: Lyft settles landmark driver misclassification lawsuit for $272.5M

discussion.body: The suit dates to May 2020, when then-Attorney General Xavier Becerra — now the Democratic candidate for governor — sued Uber and Lyft, arguing they evaded state law by declaring their drivers were not employees.
Six years from filing to a settlement that covers one of the two companies, with the other half still running. Slow is the norm in these fights, and it's the drivers who wait.

items.title: Lyft Settles California Driver Misclassification Case for $272.5 Million
items.body: California's attorney general and three city attorneys announced a $272.5 million settlement with Lyft over allegations that the company committed wage theft by classifying drivers as independent contractors rather than employees between 2016 and 2020, according to a statement cited by Ars Technica. The settlement affects only Lyft; the case against Uber continues. The allegations are the state's, and the resolution is a settlement rather than a court ruling. That is the shape most misclassification fights take: the question of who counts as an employee gets answered in money rather than doctrine, and the same question stays live on the other side of this case.

sources.title: The dawn of the age of the exoskeleton

discussion.body: Designed to increase lower-body strength, tested to see whether it improves speed and endurance — those are two different claims. Only the first is a design intent; the second is the open question.
True, and it's the open question the team cares about. The stated payoff is speed and endurance during a search for a stranded person, not a number on a bench.

items.title: Mountain Rescuers Are Testing Powered Assist Devices on the Trail
items.body: Members of Seattle Mountain Rescue have spent this year hiking into the wilderness with powered assistive devices attached to their hips and legs. The equipment is designed to increase lower-body strength when climbing or carrying heavy loads, and it is being tested to see whether it can boost rescuers' speed and endurance when it matters most — during searches for stranded people. The target of the trial is the interesting part. Not a lab measure of force, but the thing a search actually depends on: how far and how fast a team can move while carrying what it needs. Search and rescue makes a demanding test bed, because the load and the terrain are real, and the failure mode would be gear that stops earning its weight over a long day.

sources.title: Dual UK-Iranian national released on bail over suspected plot against U.S.-run military base

items.title: Sixth Person Released on Bail in Suspected Plot Near RAF Fairford
items.body: A 25-year-old man was arrested in London on Thursday on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts close to RAF Fairford, the air base that has been used by American bombers to strike Iran, PBS NewsHour reports. He was taken into custody and then released on bail. He is the sixth person to go through that sequence as detectives continue investigating the incident. Suspicion, arrest and bail are not a finding of guilt; the report describes a continuing inquiry rather than a concluded case.

sources.title: 3 Cape Bretoners were hit and killed by a train in Maine in 1970. Some want the case reopened

items.title: Three Young Men, Sleeping Bags on a Maine Rail Track, and a 1970 Death Ruled Accidental
items.body: Kenny Novak, 15, David Burrows, 17, and Terry Burt, 20, were lying in sleeping bags on a rail track west of the border town of Houlton, Maine, CBC Canada reports. Early on the morning of July 10, 1970, a train struck them. The deaths were ruled accidental. Questions about them, CBC notes, persist.

sources.title: Skydance Blasts Off: Can David Ellison Make Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Fly?

discussion.body: Calling the whole thing Skydance tells you the acquisition is being treated as an annexation, not a marriage of equals.
Or it is just brand economy — one recognisable name for a conglomerate is easier to sell than a hyphenated mashup.
Either way, Variety's own framing leaves room to read the move as swagger: bold for some readers, arrogant for others.

items.title: David Ellison Puts One Name Over Two Swallowed Studios: Skydance Corp.
items.body: David Ellison has emerged victorious, and Variety reports that he has decided to name the entertainment giant he has bolted together Skydance Corp. — a nod to the original name of the film production firm that has swallowed up two Hollywood studios over the past 14 months. Variety frames the choice as bold, or arrogant if you prefer, and credits him with defying skeptics and beating back opponents. Naming the combined entity after the acquirer is a small piece of branding that says a lot about who is expected to set the tone.

sources.title: Selma Blair Announces ‘Hineni’ Doc About Antisemitism After She Was “Erased” Over Islamophobic Comments

discussion.body: Where you announce a film is part of the film's meaning. An ADL reception is a very specific room, and choosing it does some of the arguing for her.
Or the room just tells you who the film is for. Documentaries about antisemitism have a natural constituency, and that's where it gathers — the setting may be targeting rather than testimony.

items.title: Selma Blair Channels the Fallout From Her Islamophobic Comments Into a Film About Antisemitism
items.body: More than two years after her Islamophobic comments, Selma Blair is making a documentary about antisemitism. Deadline reports that she announced the project, titled Hineni (Here I Am), on Thursday at the ADL's State of the Arts Reception in New York City, and frames it as her channeling the fallout from those comments into a film about a different form of hate speech entirely. The venue is the detail that lingers: an Anti-Defamation League arts reception rather than a festival stage or a studio announcement. Penance, a change of subject, or simply the documentary she wanted to make — the announcement doesn't settle which, and the film itself may or may not.

sources.title: Fredericton chief says police are making progress since collapse of two murder trials

items.title: Fredericton's Police Chief Says the Force Has Changed Since Two Murder Trials Collapsed
items.body: The chief of police in Fredericton says the force has made significant changes after an investigation into an error that forced the Crown to abandon two murder trials last year. Abandoning a trial ends a prosecution before a verdict, which makes it a different kind of outcome from an acquittal: neither case produced a conviction, and no jury decided anything about the accused. The chief's phrase for the response is his own — 'significant changes' describes how the force now works, offered after an error that had already cost two prosecutions.

sources.title: Growing fear of war in the Horn of Africa after Eritrea cuts ties with Ethiopia

items.title: Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt Trade Accusations as the African Union Urges Restraint
items.body: DW reports that the Tigray conflict is no longer only a domestic matter, with Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt trading accusations and the African Union urging restraint. The outlet frames the open question as whether the Horn of Africa is heading toward a wider regional crisis. Regionalization is the part worth watching. Once a conflict stops being internal, the number of parties with an interest in it multiplies, and here the mediator is appealing to governments that are simultaneously accusing one another. Restraint appeals are cheap; whether they land depends on what the accusing parties think they have to gain from escalation.

sources.title: Nova Scotia’s new EV fee raises bigger questions for drivers across Canada

discussion.body: A flat charge doesn't track use: two identical EVs, one driven a few thousand kilometres and one driven sixty thousand, pay the same $500. That's closer to a club membership than a road-use price.
The plug-in hybrid rate cuts against a pure road-use story too. A car paying half as much is still on the same pavement. Whatever the province is pricing, it isn't just distance.

items.title: Nova Scotia Adds $500 Every Two Years for EV Owners, on Top of Registration
items.body: Electric vehicle owners in Nova Scotia will now pay $500 every two years in addition to their vehicle registration fee, Global News Canada reports. Plug-in hybrid vehicles get a smaller add-on: $250 on top of registration as well. That two-tier split is the part worth sitting with. A battery-only car pays double what a plug-in hybrid pays, and neither figure varies with how much the car is actually driven. The charge may be about road upkeep, lost fuel-tax revenue, or something else again — the amounts on their own don't say, but the gap between the two categories implies a judgment about the two kinds of vehicle.

sources.title: Will Spain's housing crisis lead to a snap election?

items.title: Spain's Congress Rejected Housing Measures; Marches Are Set for Madrid
items.body: Spain's Congress rejected measures aimed at tackling the country's housing crisis, and a series of marches has been scheduled in Madrid, the BBC's Guy Hedgecoe reports from the capital. The order of those two facts is the story: the parliamentary route produced nothing on housing, and the pressure moves to the street.

sources.title: Guillermo Del Toro Buries ‘Digger’ In Praise, Slams “Petty” Review: “Decidedly A Theatrical Experience”

discussion.body: Peer praise is still a review, just from a different seat. Del Toro's endorsement carries a different weight than a studio line because he's a filmmaker with three Oscars and nothing to sell here.
Enthusiasm is cheap on social media. The critic's 'far from a must-watch' at least stakes a position on the movie itself; a post heaping praise on it doesn't tell a reader whether the satire lands.

items.title: Guillermo del Toro Praised 'Digger' — and Answered a Critic Who Said to Wait
items.body: 'Digger' premiered this weekend to mixed reviews, and Guillermo del Toro is a confirmed fan. The three-time Oscar winner took to social media to heap praise on Tom Cruise's latest, Deadline reports, after pushing back on a critic who called the Alejandro G. Iñárritu satire 'far from a must-watch' and advised waiting. A director liking a film is not news. A director putting his own name behind an answer to a critic, in public, on the film's opening weekend, is a different gesture — it moves the disagreement somewhere readers can see it instead of leaving it in a private note.

sources.title: Just short of its 200th birthday, a landmark natural history museum shuts down

items.title: Philadelphia's Academy of Natural Sciences Closes After a Fight to Save It
items.body: NPR reports that Philadelphia's Academy of Natural Sciences closed this week, after an intense fight by local residents, politicians and scientists to save it. The museum was beloved for its dinosaurs, which is the sort of collection people assume will simply always be there for the next school group and the one after that. What stands out is the coalition: neighbours, elected officials and working scientists, three groups with very different reasons to care, all arguing for the same building. A natural history museum can feel more permanent than the city around it, since its specimens are older than everyone who visits them. That is part of why a closure like this reads as a loss of something that was meant to stay put.

sources.title: ‘Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall’ Review: PTA’s Spellbinding Concert Doc Is a Gorgeously Tender Performance

discussion.body: Concert films have a built-in problem: the audience already knows the songs. Putting the director visibly in the room makes the filming itself the event.
Or the apparatus eats the performance. If the story becomes the director's camera, the singer is scenery.
Maybe the sparseness is what makes room for it. Piano arrangements this thin leave a lot of empty space, and a camera in that space is one more thing to listen around.

items.title: Paul Thomas Anderson Operates His Own Camera Onstage in a Concert Film
items.body: IndieWire's review from the New York Film Festival singles out one detail: Paul Thomas Anderson operates his own Panavision camera onstage while the Geese frontman plays and croons through hauntingly sparse piano arrangements. The setup puts the filmmaker inside the performance space rather than behind the fourth wall, so the filming itself becomes part of what is happening on stage rather than an invisible service performed for the audience. With arrangements that spare, a camera in the room may be the most conspicuous object in it — and the reviewer's enthusiasm suggests the choice reads as intimacy rather than intrusion.

sources.title: How Albertsons Companies is reimagining retail from the inside out

discussion.body: A grocery chain taking both the packaged assistant and the API is a small signal about how this lands in ordinary businesses: not one tool, but two layers — the safe one for people, the open one for experiments.

Or it's a signal about procurement rather than transformation. Buy the thing everyone has heard of, keep the API for the internal projects, and announce both. Neither layer tells us anything yet about the shopper's experience.

items.title: Albertsons Says It's Running ChatGPT Enterprise and the OpenAI API
items.body: OpenAI's own account of the work says Albertsons is using ChatGPT Enterprise and the OpenAI API to help its teams work faster and make grocery shopping easier for millions of customers. Both layers of the stack are named: the packaged assistant for staff, the API for whatever the company builds around it. The speed claim is the vendor's, attached to a customer it is proud of — the sort of claim that gets settled by whether the work actually changes, not by the case study announcing it.

sources.title: Will Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s ‘You Can See Everything’ Score a Best Picture Nomination? Not If Oscar History Is Any Guide

discussion.body: Festival breakout status and awards contention get discussed as if they were one thing. Treating them as two separate hurdles seems right: buzz is about discovery, nominations are about consensus.
Consensus is just discovery with a longer runway. The film everyone leaves the festival talking about is exactly the one that enters the race with something to build on.

items.title: A Theranos Film Is the Festival Breakout; the Oscar Races Are Another Matter
items.body: IndieWire calls the film about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes the breakout of fall festival season — and, in the same breath, sees major challenges for it in the Best Picture or Best Documentary race. Those are two different audiences doing two different jobs. A festival crowd rewards discovery; an awards campaign asks a far larger and slower group to agree. Being the thing people talked about at the festivals is an asset in that campaign, but it isn't the campaign.

sources.title: Woman told Cornell investigators she 'felt like bait' during alleged gang rape

items.title: Records in the Cornell Case Offer a Fuller Timeline, and Accounts That Don't Agree
items.body: PBS NewsHour reports that records from the Cornell investigation, while heavily redacted, offer a fuller but sometimes conflicting timeline of events and a glimpse at how the men responded to the allegations. Some disputed the woman's account, saying they weren't involved in any assault. A release like this rarely produces one clean version of a contested night; it produces more versions, each with more detail attached.

sources.title: No one expected Leo to be pope — except everyone who knew him as 'Bob'

items.title: The Conclave That Ended With an American Pope
items.body: When the 2025 conclave began, no one expected an American pope. By its end, Cardinal Robert Prevost had become Pope Leo, NPR reports. The surprise is not just who was chosen, but that the expectation at the start was so different from the outcome.

sources.title: What happened in the failed execution of Christa Pike - and what next?

items.title: Two Lethal Injections, and Christa Pike Is in a Tennessee Hospital
items.body: Christa Pike, a convicted killer, is in hospital in Tennessee after surviving two lethal injections, the BBC reports, in a case the broadcaster says has raised many questions. In a country that still carries out executions, that is not a small thing to leave hanging: a procedure designed as final did not finish the job, and it did so in front of witnesses, officials and, eventually, a court of public opinion. The word the report uses is the word that sticks. We say patients survive; we say the condemned are executed. Pike is in a hospital bed, and the case is now a set of questions rather than a conclusion.
